title: Reinforcement Learning with Pairwise Preferences in Long-Term Decision Problems
claim: Our preference-based methods learn faster and reach higher return than the baseline across long-horizon control tasks, including nontransitive ones.
layout: 2 rows: 4 learning-curve panels above, 3 panels below, shared legend
description: The figure has two groups of line plots. Row (a), labelled 'Mujoco-v5 Suite', has four learning-curve panels: Ant, Inverted Double Pendulum, Reacher and Pusher. Each plots episode return against environment steps, with shaded variance bands. Row (b), labelled 'Mujoco Nontransitive (NT) Tasks', has three panels. The first is a scatter of positions on a circle for Reacher-NT. The other two plot optimality gap against environment steps for Reacher-NT and Walker2D-NT, with error bars. A legend at the lower right maps colors to methods: PPO (gray), HPI-Clip (purple), HPI (orange-red), SPPO (green) and SPPO best-iterate (dotted green). The eye goes to the purple and orange curves rising above the green curve, which stays flat or declines.
caption: Performance of algorithms on (a) Mujoco-v5 Suite and (b) Mujoco-NT Tasks, which have long time horizons. Both HPI-Clip and HPI are more learning-efficient than SPPO on these tasks, as measured by the Area Under the Curve (AUC).
abstract: Reinforcement learning with scalar rewards is widely used for aligning machine-learning systems with user preferences. But, pairwise preferences are often more natural for users to specify than scalar rewards, and they express certain goals that scalar rewards cannot. Methods for reinforcement learning with pairwise preferences have thus received growing interest. Unfortunately, these methods are inefficient in problems with long time horizons, and they lack guarantees on the performance of Markov policies relative to history-dependent policies, which bridge the theory and practice of reinforcement learning. We address these limitations in a new problem setting for reinforcement learning with pairwise preferences called the \textit{Markov decision contest}. In this setting, we prove that stationary Markov policies perform just as well as history-dependent policies; that the problem of recovering an optimal policy exactly is in P; and that a simple iterative algorithm converges to an optimal policy at a sublinear rate. Lastly, we implement a deep-learning variant of our iterative algorithm and demonstrate its efficiency in long-term decision problems that require function approximation.
